English Bible
ING-glish BI-bul
noun phrase
The compound phrase denoting the corpus of English-language Scripture translations, beginning with John Wycliffe's hand-copied manuscripts (c. 1380–1395), the first complete English Bible, translated from the Latin Vulgate. The modern printed tradition begins with William Tyndale's New Testament (1526), translated from Erasmus's Greek text; continued through Coverdale (1535), Matthew's Bible (1537), the Great Bible (1539), the Geneva Bible (1560), and the Bishops' Bible (1568)—culminating in the King James Version of 1611, which drew on the entire tradition to produce the most influential English Bible in history.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The English Bible is the providential story of God's Word breaking into the vernacular tongue of an English-speaking people—a story inseparable from the martyrs who died to put Scripture in ordinary hands. William Tyndale, the architect of English biblical prose, translated the New Testament from Erasmus's Greek text and was strangled and burned in 1536 for doing so; his dying prayer was “Lord, open the King of England's eyes.” Within three years, an English Bible sat in every English parish by royal command—a fulfillment that displays divine sovereignty over kings and councils.

The Geneva Bible (1560), produced by English Protestant exiles under Calvin's patronage, introduced verse numbering and Calvinist annotations that shaped Puritan biblical literacy for a century. When King James I authorized a new translation in 1604, the 47 translators drew on Geneva's scholarship while setting aside its partisan notes. The resulting Authorized Version (1611)—universally called the King James Bible—synthesized the best of the Reformation tradition: Tyndale's cadences, Geneva's accuracy, and ecclesiastical stateliness, producing a text that would dominate English Protestant worship for over three centuries and carry the gospel to the ends of the earth.

Every English Bible carries the blood of martyrs and the labor of scholars who believed God's people must hear His Word in their own tongue—following the Ezra principle of reading and explaining the law so that hearers understand its meaning (Neh. 8:8).

Origin & Era

The English Bible as a category for the history of English-language Scripture translations is a modern scholarly phrase; its subject—vernacular Scripture—reflects the Reformation conviction that God's Word belongs to all His people in their own tongue.

expand to see more

The English Bible tradition begins with John Wycliffe (c. 1380), the “Morning Star of the Reformation,” who translated the entire Bible into Middle English from the Latin Vulgate; Wycliffe was condemned posthumously, his bones exhumed and burned.

William Tyndale (1494–1536) translated the New Testament from Erasmus's Greek (1526) and the Pentateuch from Hebrew (1530), giving English Christianity its foundational biblical prose; his vocabulary and cadences supplied roughly 84% of the KJV New Testament.

The Geneva Bible (1560) was the first English Bible with verse numbers, cross-references, and Calvinist marginal notes; it was the Bible of Shakespeare, the Puritans, John Bunyan, the Pilgrim Fathers, and the first century of English-speaking Reformed Christianity.

The Authorized Version (1611) was produced by 47 scholars in six companies working from the Hebrew Masoretic Text and the Greek Textus Receptus; it drew on all its predecessors and achieved a literary and theological standard that made it the defining English text for three centuries.

Modern translation proliferation (RSV 1952, NIV 1978, ESV 2001 and successors) reflects both legitimate text-critical scholarship and, in some cases, progressive gender-ideology pressures; the KJV tradition of formal equivalence from the Textus Receptus remains the dictionary's reference standard.

Key Scripture

Acts 2:6 — "And when this sound occurred, the crowd came together — and were bewildered, because each one of them was hearing them speak in his own language."

Neh. 8:8 — "And they read from the book, from the law of God, translating to give the sense so that they understood the reading."

2 Tim. 3:15 — "And how from infancy you have known the holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus."

Rom. 15:4 — "For whatever was written in earlier times was written for our instruction — so that through perseverance and the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope."

Modern Corruption

Dynamic-equivalence translation philosophy and gender-inclusive language revisions domesticate Scripture's specific words, obscure Christological typology, and produce versions shaped more by modern editorial ideology than by fidelity to the original-language texts.

expand to see more

Eugene Nida's dynamic equivalence theory (1964) introduced “meaning-for-meaning” rather than “word-for-word” translation as the governing philosophy for modern versions. The approach has merit in resolving idiom, but it became the theoretical cover for ideological revision: the 2011 NIV and the NRSVue systematically gender-neutralize the text, rendering adelphoi (brothers) as “brothers and sisters,” singular masculine pronoun chains as “they,” and generic-masculine anthropological language in ways that alter the text's meaning rather than clarify it. When Psalm 1 is changed to plural to avoid a “male-only” reading, the Messianic singular—which Jesus, Peter, and Paul applied to Christ—is erased from the version millions of evangelical churchgoers read.

The deeper corruption in popular evangelical culture is a consumerist approach to Bible versions: choosing a translation for its readability or tone rather than its fidelity to the original languages. When translations compete on accessibility rather than accuracy, the congregation is insulated from the difficulty of the text rather than trained by it. The Reformation answer is to honor the words themselves: verbum Dei manet in aeternum—the Word of God endures forever (Isa. 40:8). Formal equivalence, while demanding more of the reader, preserves the very words through which the Spirit works and through which the conscience is bound.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Rooted in the Reformation conviction that God's people must hear His Word in their own tongue, producing a two-century English translation tradition from Tyndale through the Authorized Version.

expand to see more

Old English — the earliest biblical texts in English were Caedmon's verse paraphrases (c. 680) and Bede's translation of John's Gospel (d. 735); Old English glosses between the lines of Latin Psalters date to the 8th–9th centuries

John Wycliffe (c. 1380) — first complete English Bible, translated from Jerome's Latin Vulgate by Wycliffe's circle at Oxford; hand-copied and suppressed by the established church; Wycliffe was posthumously condemned and his bones burned

William Tyndale (1526, 1530) — first printed New Testament in English (from Erasmus's Greek) and first printed Pentateuch (from Hebrew); Tyndale was strangled and burned at the stake in 1536; his translation supplied the cadences of the KJV

Geneva Bible (1560) — produced by English Protestant exiles in Geneva; first English Bible with verse numbers, italics for supplied words, and Calvinist marginal notes; the Bible of the Puritans, Shakespeare, and the Pilgrim Fathers

Authorized Version (1611) — the “King James Bible,” commissioned by James I at Hampton Court; 47 translators in six panels from the Hebrew and Greek; the defining English literary and religious monument, still the dictionary's reference standard

Usage

"Tyndale's prayer as he died—“Lord, open the King of England's eyes”—was answered within three years: every English parish was required to have a Bible in English, fulfilling the reformer's life work through the very crown that executed him."

"The Geneva Bible was so deeply Calvinist in its marginal notes that James I refused to authorize it and commissioned a new translation—yet the KJV that resulted drew heavily on Geneva's accuracy, honoring the Reformed scholarship even while setting aside its political commentary."

"Every time a preacher opens his English Bible and reads a verse, he stands on the blood of William Tyndale, whose felony was putting the same words in the language his congregation spoke."
